KEY MESSAGE 1...Rain arrives from west to east through the morning
continuing overnight.Rain exits most areas Monday morning with 
the exception of a few lingering showers near the Cape and 
Islands. 

Expect the second-half of the weekend to be a soggy one. A shortwave 
trough coupled with an 850mb jet will advect in ample moisture and 
increase lift across the region. Precipitable water values increase 
to 1.3-1.8" which equates to 160-190 percent of normal. Despite the 
anomalous moisture, weak forcing and a lack of instability will 
limit heavy rain rates, keeping the flash flood threat low. This 
event will primarily feature a prolonged period of more stratiform-
like rain driving by the WAA rather than convective downpours that 
are fueled by instability. 

High-resolution guidance shows rain likely arriving mid to late 
morning for most areas as rain spreads from west to east. Rain may 
not arrive in the more eastern parts of southern New England until 
around noon. Rain continues overnight, coming to and end between 2AM-
8AM for most areas. High-res guidance hints at the potential for 
showers to linger for the Cape and Islands through the afternoon 
(latest). 

As mentioned earlier, there isn't a strong signal for widespread 
heavy rain/downpours with this system. However, there are 
indications of very marginal instability along the south coast which 
may be enough to support an embedded rumble of thunder and a brief 
heavier rainfall. Areas of increased convergence will also be 
favored for enhanced rain rates. There are a couple areas of 
enhanced convergence as well that have been highlighted across model 
guidance with areas along the Mass Pike and higher terrain in 
western and central southern New England. These areas would at least 
be more favorable for more enhanced rates and thus higher end 
totals. 

For total amounts, HREF PMM shows a range of 0.50 to 1.2" with the 
higher end of the range being more localized and in those favored 
areas discussed above (terrain, south coast). HREF ensemble max 
shows localized amounts of 1.5-1.75" which would be a low 
probability (< 10%) given it is a max of that guidance. 
Global/ensemble guidance leans slightly lighter overall with amounts 
0.30-0.70". Outside of the localized moderate to briefly heavier 
rates, the lower rain rates should keep the flash flood threat low. 
Can't rule out some minor ponding in the usual poor drainage spots, 
but otherwise this will be prolonged soaking rain. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...High pressure will yield mainly dry conditions 
and cool temperatures the first half of the week. Potential for 
an offshore coastal low late week. There is still uncertainty in
the track and strength at this time. 

There is good agreement across model guidance with a fairly 
strong surface high shifting over Quebec Tuesday into late-week.
This will put the region under a cooler than normal airmass 
with consistent NE flow. This will yield cooler than normal 
highs in the 60s through the week. There is a low probability 
that a system just brushes southern New England Tuesday bringing
a chance for showers mainly confined to the immediate south 
coast and Cape/Islands.

Deterministic and ensemble guidance continues highlight potential 
for a slow moving offshore coastal storm developing Wednesday into 
late-week. There is a general consensus with an upper low and trough 
first tracking eastward across the upper mid-west, although cluster 
analysis does highlight some variance in the amplitude of the trough 
and track of the  low. As this pushes to the east coast, a coastal 
low develops in the Atlantic then tracking northward toward the 
northeastern coastline. As with most coastal storms this far out, 
there is still a notable amount of variance across guidance in how 
this low tracks and its strength. This will directly feed into the 
uncertainty in elements such as winds, rain chances/amounts, and 
coastal erosion/flooding concerns. 

With a strong high to the north and an incoming upper low, the 
pressure gradient will tighten Tuesday through the week. This will 
result in strengthening winds/gusts across the coastal waters, 
especially the southern waters in closer proximity to the stronger 
gradient. There is some question on how strong the gradient gets and 
where the strong part of the gradient positions and this will
likely depend on the track and strength of the low. All that 
said, ensemble guidance is signaling potential for gale force 
gusts for the southern waters. Strong gusts may develop as early
as Tuesday night, but more likely Wednesday morning. Strong 
winds are likely to stay as the coastal low tracks northward; 
however, the magnitude will depend more on the track and 
strength of the low itself which remains less certain at this 
time. For land, winds will be gusty as well although not as 
high in magnitude as the coastal waters(25-35 mph) Wed- late
